# Declared inventory of secrets that are DELIBERATELY ABSENT from the hosted app.
#
# Contract (enforced by .github/scripts/check-fly-secret-drift.py and honoured by
# the `Set all app secrets on Fly.io` step in .github/workflows/deploy-hosted.yml,
# issue #11122):
#   `fly-managed-secrets.txt` declares what the deploy MANAGES. This file declares
#   what it must NOT manage — for now, on purpose. A name recorded here is never
#   staged to Fly by a deploy, even when its GitHub Actions secret exists.
#
# Issue #11122 paid for this (measured, 2026-11-05/06). `SENTRY_DSN` was unset on
# `tortoise-y4mjjq` as the LIVE mitigation for #11092 (the source-context
# serialization storm that took api.premiselabs.co down for ~2h): with the secret
# absent `/health` answered in 0.25–1.07 s; with it present three `py-spy dump`s
# showed the MainThread parked inside `sentry_sdk` building an event. Two hosted
# deploys then landed — `42117073101` (23:13) and `42135045025` (deploy-api
# completed 01:04) — and EACH ONE PUT THE SECRET BACK, on builds (`46ea687dc`,
# `c3af2d0188`) that provably did
# NOT contain the code fix. The `Set all app secrets on Fly.io` step asserts a
# DESIRED STATE ("every declared secret exists") and so cannot tell
#
#   * "this secret is absent because nobody configured it" — the case the step
#     exists for, from
#   * "this secret is absent because an operator removed it 40 minutes ago as the
#     only thing keeping production healthy" — what actually happened.
#
# It is the stale-flag pattern from AGENTS.md: a record of a past state (the
# secret list in GitHub) applied as a measurement of the present, with no
# revalidation, silently overwriting an operational decision made with the
# incident in front of the operator. It also INVERTS the mitigation's own logic —
# the more often we deploy, the faster the mitigation is undone.
#
# ⛔ THE EXCEPTION MUST BE HONOURED AT SYNC TIME, NOT ONLY AT COMPARISON TIME.
#    A rule that only makes a gate quiet is a FALSE exception: the sync still
#    applies the declared value and the exception exists only in the report. This
#    is the measured Argo CD trap — `spec.ignoreDifferences` suppresses the
#    difference during comparison while the sync still applies the desired value,
#    so `RespectIgnoreDifferences=true` is needed for the exception to be real.
#    Here the SYNC is `flyctl secrets set` in deploy-hosted.yml, so the filter
#    lives THERE (it drops a ledgered name from the argv), and the gate's job is
#    the reverse: prove the filter actually suppressed the name, so a future edit
#    that drops the filter cannot quietly re-arm the mitigation.
#
# FORMAT — one entry per line:
#
#     <NAME> owner=<owner> expires=<YYYY-MM-DD> reason=<free text to end of line>
#
#   `#` at the START of a line is a comment. A `#` INSIDE an entry is data — the
#   reason normally cites issues (`#11092`) and stripping at the first `#` would
#   truncate exactly the field that makes the entry useful. Blank lines ignored.
#   `<owner>` is who owns the decision (a handle, not a role). `expires` is the
#   LAST day the omission is authorised, UTC. The NAME must start at COLUMN 0: the
#   sync filter takes each line's first whitespace-delimited token, so an indented
#   entry names an empty secret and would be silently ignored — the gate refuses it
#   (exit 2) rather than let the two readers disagree.
#
#   `reason` is a REVIEW note, NEVER the value: this file is tracked and public, and
#   the gate echoes every entry's reason on a clean deploy (and quotes it in
#   `MITIGATION LAPSED`).
#
# FOUR STATES FAIL THE DEPLOY (all reported by check-fly-secret-drift.py, see its
# ledger block in docs/infra-runbook.md §8.1) — an entry the machinery cannot READ,
# an entry the deploy cannot HONOUR, an entry that has LAPSED, and an entry whose
# name is LIVE on Fly:
#
#   exit 2 — the ledger cannot be READ, or cannot be HONOURED by the deploy:
#            a malformed line, leading whitespace, a missing/duplicate field, an
#            unparsable date, a duplicate NAME, a name the manifest does not
#            declare, a name declared `workflow` / `fly-toml-env` / `fly-only:`
#            (the ledger suppresses a MANAGED Fly SECRET — `gh-secret:` — not a
#            versioned value and not a decision-backed out-of-band one), a name in
#            the app's MANDATORY set, or **a ledgered name the deploy still applies**
#            (`LEDGER NOT HONOURED`, exit 2 — either the sync filter was dropped or
#            bypassed so the payload would re-arm the mitigation, or the name is also
#            assigned in `fly.toml [env]`, which the deploy applies whatever the
#            secret list says).
#            Exit 2 is never bypassable, and that is right here: a ledger the
#            machinery cannot honour is worse than no ledger, because the entry
#            reads as a decision while the deploy does the opposite. It is also why
#            `LEDGER NOT HONOURED` is exit 2 and not exit 1 — exit 1 is the
#            documented `skip-fly-secret-provenance` lane, and an operator arming
#            that for an unrelated stale declaration must not thereby re-stage
#            every mitigation here.
#   exit 1 — the entry is stale: it has EXPIRED (re-affirm it with a new expiry,
#            or delete it so the deploy resumes managing the secret), or its name
#            EXISTS on Fly (the omission is not in effect — unset the secret, or
#            delete the entry; while both are true the entry also freezes the
#            value, so a rotation in GitHub would silently not propagate).
#            ⛔ Exit 1 is BYPASSABLE by design (`skip-fly-secret-provenance`), and
#            the bypass's report talks only about secret DECLARATIONS — it will not
#            tell you that a lapsed entry keeps suppressing in the meantime.
#
# ⛔ AN EXPIRED ENTRY KEEPS SUPPRESSING. That is deliberate: the alternative is to
#    silently re-arm on a date, which is the same unannounced overwrite with extra
#    steps. The deploy goes RED instead, and the remedy is one line either way.
#
# ⛔ WHY A MANDATORY NAME IS REFUSED. `FASTAPI_INTERNAL_KEY`, `TORTOISE_SECRET_PEPPER`,
#    `FALKORDB_CLOUD_URI` (the API cannot boot) and `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`,
#    `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` (billing must not ship silently dead) already hard-fail
#    the deploy in `Verify secrets exist`. Removing one of those is not a
#    mitigation, it is an outage, and an entry here would make the machinery
#    cooperate with the outage. (`SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN` and `FLY_API_TOKEN` are
#    hard-required there too but are never Fly secrets, so the manifest
#    declaration rule already refuses them.)
#
# HOW TO RECORD A MITIGATION (the incident path):
#   1. `flyctl secrets unset <NAME> -a tortoise-y4mjjq` — do the mitigating thing
#      first; the ledger records what you did, it does not do it.
#   2. Add the entry below, in the same PR that would otherwise re-arm it, with
#      the INCIDENT number in `reason` and an `expires` you are willing to defend.
#   The next deploy reports the name as MITIGATED in the provenance gate and
#   stages nothing for it.
#
# ⛔ THERE IS A WINDOW BETWEEN 1 AND 2, AND IT IS NOT COVERED. The filter knows a
#    name only once the ENTRY has merged, so between the `unset` and the merge a push
#    to `main` re-stages the secret from its GitHub secret — which is #11122 verbatim,
#    once per mitigation. Do NOT read the order above as "removal first, protection
#    follows". Land the entry in the same window and treat "no deploy to `main` until
#    this merges" as part of the mitigation; if one does go out, the belt warning
#    below is the only cover and the deploy has ALREADY put the secret back (re-do
#    step 1 afterwards). The reverse order does not help either: an entry for a name
#    that is still on Fly fails the deploy (exit 1 `MITIGATION NOT IN EFFECT`).
#
# ⚠️ ONE MORE PATH IS NOT CLOSED, and it is RECORDED here rather than assumed away.
#    This deploy uses `flyctl secrets set --stage`, which leaves the change PENDING
#    until a `flyctl deploy` applies it. If a run stages <NAME> and then fails before
#    the release, that pending stage may survive, and a later run — this time with the
#    entry in force, so nothing is staged — would still apply it during `flyctl
#    deploy`. Nothing here reads or clears pending staged state. **The one question
#    that was open here is now SETTLED:** `flyctl secrets list --json` (what this gate
#    reads) LISTS a staged secret as present with a `Staged` deployment status (Fly
#    docs, `fly secrets list`), so the entry fails the deploy loudly with `MITIGATION
#    NOT IN EFFECT` instead of the value being applied unnoticed — and the provenance
#    gate runs ahead of `flyctl deploy` in the same `deploy-api` job, so that red
#    stops the run that would have applied the stage. ⛔ What remains is that this is
#    **exit 1**, the bypassable class: `skip-fly-secret-provenance` armed for an
#    unrelated declaration applies the pending value silently, and the entry freezes
#    rotation while it stands. Clear the stage before re-running (see runbook §8.1).
#
# HOW TO RESTORE: delete the entry (the deploy resumes managing the name from its
#   GitHub secret on the next run), or — if the value must come back out-of-band
#   first — `flyctl secrets set <NAME>=… -a tortoise-y4mjjq` and THEN delete the
#   entry, because an entry whose name exists on Fly fails the deploy.
#
# ⛔ THE FALLBACK IS NOT SILENT (the belt). Independently of this file, the gate
#    WARNS on every deploy that would CREATE a secret currently absent from the
#    app — "absent and unledgered reads as never configured", so an operator who
#    was firefighting and never wrote the entry still gets told, before the
#    mutation, which names are about to be restored and where to record them.
#    That is the case this file cannot cover by construction: the entry exists for
#    the removals somebody remembered.

# ── ENTRIES ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# None — and that is a DECISION to re-check, not a measurement of production.
#
# The two deploys that motivated this file (#11092's `SENTRY_DSN`, unset as the live
# mitigation) are recorded above; both put the secret back. That restoration is
# RECORDED HERE AS A RECOLLECTION: no `flyctl secrets list -a tortoise-y4mjjq`
# reading is attached to it, and the gate's ledger check is PRESENCE-only —
# `MITIGATION NOT IN EFFECT` fires when a ledgered name IS on Fly, while an ABSENT
# name with no entry produces only the belt's `::warning::`, never a verdict. So an
# empty ledger is not a claim that no mitigation is in force: it is the absence of
# any entry, and an in-force removal nobody wrote down is exactly the state the belt
# speaks about on the next deploy rather than a state this file rules out.
#
# ⛔ Before acting on "there is nothing to suppress today", READ THE FLY APP. One
#    `flyctl secrets list -a tortoise-y4mjjq` settles it, and if `SENTRY_DSN` (or any
#    other name this file's motivating incident touched) is absent, WRITE THE ENTRY
#    in that same window — an unledgered absent name is re-staged by the next deploy.
#
# An entry written to demonstrate the FORMAT would be a false record of a production
# state, so none is shipped: the first real entry is written by the operator who
# performs the removal.
